etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English waterfal, waterfalle, from Old English wæterġefeall (“waterfall”), equivalent to water +‎ fall. Cognate with West Frisian wetterfal (“waterfall”), Dutch waterval (“waterfall”), German Wasserfall (“waterfall”), Swedish vattenfall (“waterfall”).

definitions.definition: A flow of water over the edge of a cliff.
(figuratively) A waterfall-like outpouring of liquid, smoke, etc.
(slang, US) The action of drinking from a vessel without touching it with the lips, considered more sanitary for a shared vessel.

quote.citation: 1870–1871 (date written), Mark Twain [pseudonym; Samuel Langhorne Clemens], chapter LXXIX, in Roughing It, Hartford, Conn.: American Publishing Company [et al.], published 1872, →OCLC, pages 569–570:
quote.text: I found home a dreary place after my long absence; for half the children I had known were now wearing whiskers or waterfalls,  […]
Rain ran off the bill of his fielder's cap and waterfalled in front of his face.

quote.citation: 1999, Jane Yolen with Bruce Coville, Armageddon Summer, page 79:
quote.text: Zondra, whose dirty-blond hair waterfalled above her head from a colorful tie, gave a snorting, horsey kind of laugh.

quote.citation: 2008, John Gardner, No Human Enemy, page 156:
quote.text: they turned into the drive of The Manor with its red-brick front and the wonderful cloak of Virginia creeper waterfalling down between the windows.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To drink (something) from a container by pouring it from a height so as not to touch one's lips to the rim.
